questions.q: Which pharmaceutical company put heroin on the market in 1898 as a cough remedy and 'non-addictive' morphine substitute?
questions.note: Same people who brought you aspirin. One of those worked out.

questions.q: Coca-Cola stopped using fresh coca leaves, and with them most of the cocaine, in roughly what year?
questions.note: They used 'spent' leaves after that. Spent, like your uncle on Christmas Eve.

questions.q: Pervitin, handed out to German soldiers by the millions in World War II, was which drug?
questions.note: Blitzkrieg had a secret ingredient, and it was tweaking.

questions.q: Until 1948, 7 Up contained which mood stabilizer in its formula?
questions.note: The 'Up' was doing a lot of work.

questions.q: Fentanyl was first synthesized around 1960 by which Belgian chemist?
questions.note: His company still makes it. Legally, mostly.

questions.q: The FDA approved naloxone for opioid overdose in what year?
questions.note: It took another five decades to put it on a gas station shelf.

questions.q: 'Krokodil,' the Russian street drug that rots skin into scales around the injection site, is which opioid?
questions.note: Homemade from codeine, gasoline, and whatever was under the sink.

questions.q: Albert Hofmann first synthesized LSD in what year, five years before he accidentally dosed himself?
questions.note: He biked home afterward. There's a holiday for it.

questions.q: AA co-founder Bill Wilson personally experimented in the 1950s with which drug as a possible aid to recovery?
questions.note: This does not come up at the Tuesday meeting.

questions.q: Alcoholics Anonymous was founded in 1935 in which city?
questions.note: Two drunks and a kitchen table in Ohio. Twelve steps later, here we are.

questions.q: Methadone was first developed in the late 1930s in which country?
questions.note: Not named after Hitler. That rumor is a lie your sponsor told you.

questions.q: Kratom comes from a tree in the same botanical family as which everyday plant?
questions.note: Both sold at the gas station, both ruin your sleep, only one ruins your liver.

questions.q: Which of these is a Schedule II drug still prescribed in the US under the brand name Desoxyn?
questions.note: Approved for ADHD and obesity. Your doctor will not write it.

questions.q: Which drug is legally used by US surgeons as a topical anesthetic in nose and throat procedures?
questions.note: Schedule II. The ENT has a locked box and a straight face.

questions.q: In the UK, heroin is legally prescribed for severe pain under what name?
questions.note: The NHS will give you heroin. You just have to be dying correctly.

questions.q: Withdrawal from which of these drugs can, by itself, kill you?
questions.note: Heroin withdrawal makes you want to die. Alcohol withdrawal does it for you.

questions.q: 'Wet brain,' or Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, is caused by a deficiency of which vitamin?
questions.note: Hence the banana bag. Hence the yellow IV. Hence the guy who thinks it's 1994.

questions.q: Carfentanil, found in street heroin, was developed as a tranquilizer for which animals?
questions.note: About 10,000 times the potency of morphine. You are not an elephant.

questions.q: Xylazine, 'tranq,' is a sedative approved only for which use?
questions.note: Narcan doesn't touch it. Neither should you.

questions.q: Who won the 1949 Nobel Prize in Medicine for inventing the lobotomy?
questions.note: The Nobel committee has never taken it back.

questions.q: Walter Freeman's quick 'transorbital' lobotomy went in through the eye socket using what tool?
questions.note: From his own kitchen, originally. Ten minutes a patient.

questions.q: The original 'Body Farm,' where donated corpses decompose for forensic research, is run by which university?
questions.note: Behind the hospital in Knoxville. Great place to get your steps in.

questions.q: In what year did the American Psychiatric Association remove homosexuality from the DSM?
questions.note: Caffeine withdrawal is still in there.

questions.q: Which of these is an official DSM-5 diagnosis?
questions.note: Yes. Your Monday headache is billable.

questions.q: What over-the-counter drug is the leading cause of acute liver failure in the US?
questions.note: Tylenol. The one your detox roommate took twelve of for a hangover.

questions.q: Viagra was originally developed to treat what?
questions.note: Trial subjects reported a side effect. Pfizer pivoted.

questions.q: Rogaine's active ingredient, minoxidil, was originally approved as a pill for what?
questions.note: Patients got hairy. Marketing got ideas.

questions.q: In the 1920s and 30s, Lysol was heavily marketed to American women as what?
questions.note: Ads winked that it prevented pregnancy. It prevented tissue.

questions.q: Listerine's 1920s ads invented a medical-sounding condition to sell mouthwash. What was it?
questions.note: The word for bad breath was a marketing campaign. So was your self-esteem.

questions.q: Mrs. Winslow's Soothing Syrup, sold for teething babies in the 1800s, contained what?
questions.note: The AMA filed it under 'Baby Killers.' It kept selling.

questions.q: JFK's 'Dr. Feelgood,' Max Jacobson, injected the president with what?
questions.note: Thirty-four White House visits by 1962. Camelot was speeding.

questions.q: Where in Graceland was Elvis found dead in 1977?
questions.note: Face down on the floor. The King died a commoner's death.

questions.q: Dancer Isadora Duncan died in 1927 when what got caught in a car's wheel?
questions.note: Broke her neck instantly. Fashion kills, but usually slower.

questions.q: What actually killed 'Mama' Cass Elliot in 1974, despite the famous rumor?
questions.note: Her manager planted the sandwich story because it sounded better than drugs.

questions.q: Commercial bail bondsmen exist almost exclusively in the US and which other country?
questions.note: Everywhere else looked at it and said no.

questions.q: The first US drug court opened in 1989 in which county?
questions.note: Born of the crack era. Still handing out court cards.

questions.q: Eating a bagel topped with which seed can trigger a positive opiate drug test?
questions.note: Your PO has heard this one. It happens to be true.

questions.q: A 2009 study found cocaine traces on roughly what share of US paper money?
questions.note: Your twenty has done more coke than you.

questions.q: Which kitchen spice can cause hallucinations in large doses thanks to myristicin?
questions.note: Three tablespoons and a very bad two days. Ask any bored sober-house resident.

questions.q: 'Bath salts' are synthetic versions of a stimulant found in which plant?
questions.note: Chewed in East Africa for centuries. Smoked in a Walmart parking lot for one decade.

questions.q: PCP was first marketed by Parke-Davis in the 1950s as what?
questions.note: Patients woke up screaming. Ketamine replaced it.

questions.q: Before it was a club drug, GHB was sold in the US in 1990 as what?
questions.note: The FDA said stop in November. People did not stop.

questions.q: Quaaludes were moved to Schedule I in what year?
questions.note: Disco biscuits, 714s, Lemmons. Your dad knows the lyrics.

questions.q: Which scientist coined the term 'laughing gas' after inhaling nitrous oxide himself in 1799?
questions.note: He threw parties around it. Nurses still do, allegedly.

questions.q: Absinthe was banned in the United States from 1912 until what year?
questions.note: Ninety-five years. The green fairy did more time than most dealers.

questions.q: Four Loko removed which ingredient from its formula in late 2010?
questions.note: The FDA called it an unsafe food additive. Your freshman year called it dinner.

questions.q: The first drunk-driving arrest, in London in 1897, involved a man driving what?
questions.note: George Smith, 20 shillings. Electric cars were ruining lives before Tesla.

questions.q: From 1952 to 1956, Kent cigarettes' 'Micronite' filter contained what?
questions.note: The healthy cigarette. Crocidolite, the most carcinogenic kind.

questions.q: According to HRSA, one organ donor can save up to how many lives?
questions.note: Your liver may not be invited.

questions.q: Which US state was the first to legalize human composting in 2019?
questions.note: Thirty days later you're topsoil. Finally useful.

questions.q: Hunter S. Thompson's ashes were shot out of a cannon in 2005. Who paid for it?
questions.note: About three million dollars. The fist-shaped tower was 153 feet.

questions.q: Ozzy Osbourne bit the head off a bat onstage in 1982 in which city?
questions.note: He thought it was rubber. The rabies shots were not.

questions.q: River Phoenix died in 1993 on the sidewalk outside which club?
questions.note: Halloween night. Johnny Depp co-owned the club.

questions.q: What drug did the coroner name as the cause of Michael Jackson's death?
questions.note: A surgical anesthetic, at home, for sleep. His cardiologist did two years.

questions.q: Whitney Houston drowned in a bathtub in 2012 at which hotel?
questions.note: The night before Clive Davis's Grammy party, in the same building.

questions.q: Which of these musicians did NOT die at 27?
questions.note: Elvis made it to 42. Then the bathroom.

questions.q: A '5150' is a 72-hour involuntary psychiatric hold under the law of which state?
questions.note: Florida's version is the Baker Act. Same vibe, more humidity.

questions.q: Florida's involuntary psychiatric hold law is known as what?
questions.note: Named for a state rep, not a pastry. Up to 72 hours.

questions.q: In 1887, which journalist faked insanity to get committed and expose a New York asylum?
questions.note: 'Ten Days in a Mad-House.' Got out faster than most of your clients.

questions.q: Prozac got its FDA approval in what year?
questions.note: Eli Lilly launched it a month later. The 90s were on their way.

questions.q: Australian psychiatrist John Cade discovered lithium calms mania by first injecting it into what?
questions.note: He also injected the guinea pigs with patients' urine. Science was loose in 1948.

questions.q: Valium was the top-selling drug in America for roughly which years?
questions.note: Two billion tablets in 1978 alone. Mother's little helper, indeed.

questions.q: The Rolling Stones' 'Mother's Little Helper' is about a housewife hooked on what?
questions.note: 1966. The pills are still little. The mothers are still tired.

questions.q: Ketamine is in which DEA schedule?
questions.note: Same tier as Tylenol with codeine. The clinic charges like it's gold.

questions.q: A UC San Diego study of US death certificates found more people die on which day than any other?
questions.note: December 26 and January 1 come next. Happy holidays.

questions.q: Ernesto Miranda, of Miranda rights fame, died in 1976 how?
questions.note: The suspect fled to Mexico and was never found. You have the right to remain missing.

questions.q: The 'Twinkie defense' was coined by reporters covering whose 1979 murder trial?
questions.note: He killed Harvey Milk and the mayor. Lawyers argued depression. The snack cake got blamed.

questions.q: In 1987, Canadian Kenneth Parks drove 12 miles, killed his mother-in-law, and was acquitted. His defense?
questions.note: Five neurologists backed him. Canada's Supreme Court agreed. Sleep well.

questions.q: The last public execution in the United States was a hanging in 1936 in which state?
questions.note: Twenty thousand people showed up in Owensboro to watch.

questions.q: The electric chair was invented by a man whose day job was what?
questions.note: Alfred Southwick. He saw a drunk die touching a generator and thought: humane.

questions.q: Alabama carried out the first-ever execution by nitrogen gas in which year?
questions.note: Kenneth Smith had already survived a botched lethal injection. Second time was the charm.

questions.q: 1920s quack John Brinkley got rich transplanting what into men to cure impotence?
questions.note: He ran for governor of Kansas twice. Nearly won.

questions.q: Radithor, a 1920s radium-water tonic, famously made a steel magnate's what fall off?
questions.note: The Wall Street Journal headline: 'The Radium Water Worked Fine Until His Jaw Came Off.'

questions.q: The 'Radium Girls' were poisoned because their bosses told them to do what with their paintbrushes?
questions.note: Glowing dials, glowing jaws. The company said it was harmless.

questions.q: Julius Wagner-Jauregg won the 1927 Nobel Prize for treating syphilis by infecting patients with what?
questions.note: The fever burned out the syphilis. It also killed about 15 percent of them.

questions.q: Castoreum, historically used in vanilla and raspberry flavoring, comes from which part of a beaver?
questions.note: FDA says it's generally recognized as safe. Your taste buds say nothing.

questions.q: Which animal population in Australia is suffering a widespread chlamydia epidemic?
questions.note: There is a vaccine program. For the koalas.

questions.q: The real 'Cocaine Bear' of 1985 is now taxidermied and on display where?
questions.note: It absorbed three or four grams. The rest of the 75 pounds was just for show.

questions.q: Pablo Escobar's escaped pet hippos now number roughly how many in Colombia?
questions.note: Four hippos, one zoo, forty years. Invasive, horny, and bulletproof to policy.

questions.q: The 1982 Chicago Tylenol murders used which poison?
questions.note: Nobody was ever convicted. Every pill bottle you've fought open since is because of this.

questions.q: The 1970s 'Rat Park' experiments found rats in an enriched colony did what with morphine water?
questions.note: Lonely caged rats got hooked. Rats with friends and toys didn't. Draw your own conclusions.

questions.q: Jennifer Strange died in 2007 of water intoxication during a radio contest to win what?
questions.note: 'Hold Your Wee for a Wii.' She was 28. The console retailed for $250.

questions.q: Pitcher Dock Ellis threw a 1970 no-hitter while, by his own account, on what?
questions.note: He said he couldn't see the batter. The ball, he said, was fine.

questions.q: Len Bias died of a cocaine overdose two days after being drafted by which NBA team?
questions.note: The 1986 drug law that followed carries his name. So does a lot of federal time.

questions.q: The 1986 crack-vs-powder cocaine sentencing ratio of 100-to-1 was reduced in 2010 to what?
questions.note: Progress, as defined by Congress.

questions.q: Which country decriminalized personal possession of all drugs in 2001?
questions.note: Overdoses dropped. America took notes and lost them.

questions.q: North America's first legal supervised injection site, Insite, opened in 2003 in which city?
questions.note: Downtown Eastside. Clean needles, trained staff, no funerals that day.

questions.q: Antabuse's alcohol reaction was first noticed in workers in which industry?
questions.note: Danish scientists then tested it on themselves. They called their group the Death Battalion.

questions.q: Marilyn Monroe died in 1962 of an overdose of what class of drugs?
questions.note: Nembutal and chloral hydrate. The coroner wrote 'probable suicide.'

questions.q: Prince died in 2016 from fentanyl in counterfeit pills stamped to look like what?
questions.note: Hydrocodone on the label, fentanyl inside. Same deal as the guy in bed 4.

questions.q: Hydrocodone combination products like Vicodin were moved from Schedule III to Schedule II in what year?
questions.note: Eighteen years after OxyContin. Right on time.

questions.q: Oxycodone was first synthesized in 1916 in which country?
questions.note: Frankfurt. Purdue just put a time-release coat on it eighty years later.

questions.q: Tianeptine, sold in smoke shops as a 'supplement,' is nicknamed what?
questions.note: Approved for depression in France. Approved for nothing in the US. Sold next to the beef jerky.

questions.q: Which was the last US state to repeal statewide alcohol prohibition, in 1966?
questions.note: Thirty-three years after everyone else. Still has dry counties.

questions.q: 'Jake leg,' which paralyzed tens of thousands of Americans in 1930, came from drinking what?
questions.note: A patent medicine loophole during Prohibition. The additive ate their nerves.

questions.q: Methamphetamine was first synthesized in 1893 in which country?
questions.note: Nagai Nagayoshi, from ephedrine. Crystal came in 1919, also Japan.

questions.q: Morphine is named after Morpheus, the Greek god of what?
questions.note: Isolated in 1804 by a German pharmacist who tested it on himself.

questions.q: Utah lowered its legal driving BAC limit in 2018 to what, the strictest in the nation?
questions.note: Two beers and you're a case number.

questions.q: Over-the-counter Narcan nasal spray was approved by the FDA in what year?
questions.note: Fifty-two years after the prescription version. Now it's next to the Advil.

questions.q: Which of these is a manner of death a US medical examiner can officially check on a death certificate?
questions.note: Natural, accident, suicide, homicide, undetermined. 'Deserved' is implied.

questions.q: The 'Son of Sam' laws, which stop convicts from profiting off books and movies about their crimes, were first passed in New York because of which killer?
questions.note: Passed in 1977 before he'd sold a word. Publishers were already circling.

questions.q: Norway's maximum prison sentence, handed to a man who killed 77 people in 2011, is how long?
questions.note: Extendable five years at a time if he's still dangerous. He will be.

questions.q: In 2010, which state carried out the first US firing-squad execution since 1996?
questions.note: Ronnie Lee Gardner chose it himself. Five rifles, one loaded with a blank.

questions.q: How many times did Ted Bundy escape from custody in Colorado in 1977?
questions.note: Courthouse window in June, jail ceiling in December. Florida caught him on a traffic stop.

questions.q: The 1973 hostage crisis that gave us the term 'Stockholm syndrome' happened during a robbery of what?
questions.note: Six days in a vault. The hostages later raised money for their captors' defense.

questions.q: Which is the only crime specifically defined in the US Constitution?
questions.note: Article III, Section 3. Two witnesses or a confession in open court. Fewer than 40 ever charged.

questions.q: The 1932 'Lindbergh Law' made which crime a federal offense when it crosses state lines?
questions.note: Passed weeks after the baby was found dead. Marked ransom bills caught the guy.

questions.q: Al Capone's older brother Vincenzo changed his name and spent the 1920s working as what?
questions.note: Richard 'Two-Gun' Hart, busting bootleggers in Nebraska while his brother ran Chicago.

questions.q: Jeffrey Dahmer was killed in prison in 1994 by an inmate wielding what?
options: A metal bar from the gym
questions.note: Christopher Scarver said Dahmer shaped his prison food to look like severed limbs.

questions.q: Which serial killer's last words before his 1994 execution were reportedly 'Kiss my ass'?
questions.note: Thirty-three victims, zero remorse. His brain was removed for study. It was normal.

questions.q: The DEA was created in 1973 by which president?
questions.note: He also declared drugs 'public enemy number one.' An aide later said it was about hippies.

questions.q: New York's Rikers Island jail is named after a family whose most notorious member, Richard Riker, did what as a judge?
options: Sent free Black New Yorkers south into slavery
questions.note: The 'Kidnapping Club,' 1830s. Abolitionists coined the name. The jail kept his.

questions.q: France carried out its last execution by guillotine in what year?
questions.note: Same year Star Wars came out. Hamida Djandoubi, Marseille, behind closed doors.

questions.q: Under a law from 1872 that is still on the books, it is technically illegal in England to be drunk where?
questions.note: Licensing Act 1872, section 12. Every pub in the country is a crime scene by 9pm.

questions.q: In 1518, hundreds of people in which city danced uncontrollably for weeks, some reportedly until they died?
questions.note: The city's cure was to hire musicians and build a stage. It made things worse.

questions.q: In 1919, a 2-million-gallon wave of molasses killed 21 people in which US city?
questions.note: The tank burst in the North End. Locals swore you could smell it on hot days for decades.

questions.q: George Washington's doctors treated his final illness in 1799 by draining roughly what share of his blood in under a day?
questions.note: Four bleedings, plus blistering and an enema. He had a sore throat.

questions.q: President Garfield survived his 1881 shooting for 80 days. What most likely killed him?
options: The bullet lodged in his spine
His doctors probing the wound with unwashed fingers
questions.note: His assassin's defense: 'The doctors killed him. I just shot him.' Hanged anyway.

questions.q: London's 'Great Stink' of 1858 shut down Parliament. What caused it?
options: Raw sewage cooking in the Thames
questions.note: Curtains soaked in chloride of lime didn't help. They built the sewers after that.

questions.q: In the 1700s, Londoners paid admission to tour which institution for entertainment?
questions.note: Bedlam. Visitors poked patients with sticks. It's where the word comes from.

questions.q: During Prohibition, the US government ordered manufacturers to add what to industrial alcohol to stop people drinking it?
questions.note: People drank it anyway. An estimated 10,000 died. The policy continued.

questions.q: Immediately after Rasputin was murdered in 1916, his killers did what with his body?
options: Dropped it through the ice into a river
questions.note: Poisoned, shot, beaten, then dumped. The autopsy said the bullets did it.

questions.q: In 897, Pope Stephen VI had his predecessor Formosus dug up and did what with the corpse?
questions.note: The Cadaver Synod. A deacon answered for the body. It lost.

questions.q: In 1184, dozens of German nobles meeting in Erfurt died when a floor collapsed and dropped them into what?
questions.note: Drowned in latrine. The king survived by clinging to a window niche.

questions.q: Sweden's King Adolf Frederick died in 1771 after a huge meal that reportedly ended with 14 servings of what?
questions.note: Lobster, caviar, sauerkraut, champagne, then the buns. Swedes call him the king who ate himself to death.

questions.q: Astronomer Tycho Brahe lost part of his nose in a 1566 duel fought over what?
questions.note: He wore a metal nose for life. Legend says he died from refusing to leave a banquet to pee.

questions.q: In the CIA's 'Operation Midnight Climax,' agents dosed unwitting men with LSD after luring them with what?
questions.note: Safehouses in San Francisco, two-way mirrors, taxpayer-funded. The 1950s and 60s.

questions.q: In 1998, renovators found more than 1,200 human bones buried under whose former London home?
questions.note: A friend ran an illegal anatomy school in the basement. Probably. Franklin was 'out of town.'

questions.q: The Hatfield-McCoy feud's first courtroom fight, in 1878, was over who owned what?
questions.note: The witness who testified about the pig was murdered two years later. Over the pig.

questions.q: Which US president personally led troops into the field while in office, to put down a 1794 tax revolt over whiskey?
questions.note: The Whiskey Rebellion. The only sitting president to command an army in the field.

questions.q: Plague doctors' beaked masks were stuffed with what?
questions.note: To block 'bad air.' The disease came from fleas. The beak did nothing but look great.

questions.q: Giles Corey, accused of witchcraft at Salem in 1692, was executed how?
questions.note: Took two days. His only recorded words: 'More weight.'

questions.q: Lincoln's bodyguard at Ford's Theatre, John Parker, was away from his post doing what when Booth walked in?
options: Drinking at the saloon next door
questions.note: He was never disciplined. He kept his job, guarding Mary Lincoln.

questions.q: The shortest war in history, Britain vs. Zanzibar in 1896, lasted roughly how long?
questions.note: The sultan fled to the German consulate. One British sailor was wounded.

questions.q: In 1726, Englishwoman Mary Toft fooled the king's surgeons into believing she had given birth to what?
questions.note: Several of them, in pieces. She'd been inserting them. The doctors published first, checked later.

questions.q: In Tasmania, wallabies have been caught breaking into licensed farms, eating what, and hopping in circles?
questions.note: Tasmania grows about half the world's legal opiate crop. The wallabies know.

questions.q: Male antechinus, a small Australian marsupial, die every year after doing what?
options: Mating for up to 14 hours at a stretch for weeks
questions.note: Stress hormones wreck their immune systems. Fur falling out, bleeding internally, still at it.

questions.q: Which of these animals is physically unable to vomit?
questions.note: A strong one-way valve into the stomach. Eat something bad and it's colic or death.

questions.q: A turkey vulture's main defense against a threat is to do what?
questions.note: Half-digested roadkill, several feet. It also poops on its own legs to cool down.

questions.q: Male sea otters off California have been documented forcibly mating with, and killing, what?
questions.note: Nineteen cases in one study. Nature's cuddliest mascot has a record.

questions.q: A 1915 report on Adelie penguins' sex lives was so disturbing to its author that it was what?
options: Kept out of print for nearly 100 years
questions.note: Necrophilia, coercion, abuse of chicks. He wrote the worst parts in Greek letters.

questions.q: The Argentine lake duck holds the vertebrate record for penis length relative to body size. About how long?
questions.note: Corkscrew-shaped, brush-tipped, used like a lasso. The duck itself is about 16 inches.

questions.q: A male honeybee dies shortly after mating because what happens?
options: The queen bites his head off
His genitals rip off inside the queen
questions.note: The next drone has to pull the previous guy's parts out first. Romance.

questions.q: Dutch biologist Kees Moeliker won an Ig Nobel Prize for documenting a mallard duck doing what for 75 minutes?
questions.note: The dead duck had hit his museum window. There is now an annual Dead Duck Day.

questions.q: Hippos mark territory by doing what while they poop?
options: Spinning their tails like a propeller
questions.note: Zookeepers call it muck-spreading. Stand well back.

questions.q: Which animal produces cube-shaped poop?
questions.note: Up to 100 cubes a night, stacked to mark territory. Science figured out how in 2018.

questions.q: Which US animal can give humans leprosy?
questions.note: A chunk of US leprosy cases trace back to them. Don't eat them. People eat them.

questions.q: The cat parasite Toxoplasma gondii changes rat behavior how?
options: Makes them attracted to cat urine
questions.note: Rat walks up to cat, gets eaten, parasite breeds in cat. Roughly a third of humans carry it.

questions.q: Lobsters urinate from where?
questions.note: Nozzles under the antennae. They pee at each other to flirt and to fight.

questions.q: A male giraffe checks whether a female is ready to mate by doing what?
questions.note: He nudges her until she pees, then gargles it. It's called the flehmen response.

questions.q: After a male deep-sea anglerfish finds a mate, what happens to him?
options: He fuses to her body permanently
questions.note: His organs dissolve, their blood merges, and he becomes a sperm pouch she carries around.

questions.q: An unspayed female ferret that doesn't mate can die. Why?
options: She stays in heat and estrogen poisons her bone marrow
questions.note: Aplastic anemia. The fix is spaying, a hormone shot, or a vasectomized male. That's a job title.

questions.q: Sloths climb down from their trees roughly once a week to do what?
questions.note: They lose up to a third of their body weight doing it. Many get eaten on the trip.

questions.q: In World War II, psychologist B.F. Skinner trained which animal to guide missiles by pecking at a screen?
questions.note: Project Pigeon. It worked in tests. The military cut it anyway.

questions.q: The US military's WWII 'Project X-Ray' planned to firebomb Japanese cities using what?
questions.note: Test bats escaped and burned down a US air base in New Mexico. Project cancelled.

questions.q: In the 1960s, the CIA spent millions surgically wiring what animal with a microphone to spy on Soviets?
questions.note: Acoustic Kitty. The cat wandered off whenever it felt like it. Project abandoned.

questions.q: A rabbit hunt staged for Napoleon in 1807 went wrong when the rabbits did what?
questions.note: Hundreds of tame rabbits thought he had food. He fled to his carriage.

questions.q: Tasmanian devils are being wiped out by a cancer that spreads how?
questions.note: One of a handful of contagious cancers known. The devils bite faces constantly. Bad combination.

questions.q: Santino, a chimp at a Swedish zoo, made headlines in 2009 for calmly doing what each morning?
options: Picking the lock on his cage
Stockpiling rocks to throw at visitors
questions.note: He hid them under hay and behind logs. Scientists called it evidence of planning.

questions.q: Stubbs, honorary mayor of Talkeetna, Alaska for about 20 years, was a what?
questions.note: A write-in protest vote. Drank catnip water from a margarita glass at the bar daily.

questions.q: In 1903, Topsy the elephant was publicly killed at Coney Island by what method?
questions.note: 6,600 volts, filmed by Edison's company. They fed her cyanide-laced carrots first.

questions.q: In Switzerland, it is illegal to own just one of which pet?
questions.note: Social animals need company by law. A rental service supplies a friend when one dies.

questions.q: Under a Texas law still on the books, owning how many or more 'obscene devices' is presumed to mean you're selling them?
questions.note: A federal court struck it down in 2008. Texas never repealed it. Five is personal, six is a business.

questions.q: The first condom commercial on US network television aired in 1991 on which network?
questions.note: During 'Herman's Head.' The big three held out for years.

questions.q: The 2015 hack of which website dumped data on roughly 32 million users seeking affairs?
questions.note: Slogan: 'Life is short. Have an affair.' Most of the women turned out to be bots.

questions.q: In 2017, the maker of the We-Vibe smart vibrator paid millions to settle a lawsuit over doing what?
options: Secretly collecting data on when and how it was used
questions.note: Temperature, intensity, timestamps, all sent to Canada. Up to $10,000 each for app users.

questions.q: Nevada's legal brothels are only allowed in counties with populations under what?
questions.note: Which rules out Las Vegas. Everything there is illegal and happening anyway.

questions.q: A 28,000-year-old polished stone phallus was dug up in 2005 in a cave in which country?
questions.note: Eight inches of siltstone. Archaeologists say it may also have been used to knap flint. Sure.

questions.q: An ancient Egyptian medical papyrus recommended which contraceptive?
questions.note: Kahun Papyrus, around 1800 BC. Mixed with fermented dough. It may have sort of worked.

questions.q: The Italians called syphilis 'the French disease.' What did the French call it?
questions.note: Russians called it the Polish disease. Poles called it the German disease. Nobody owned it.

questions.q: The first US state to legally marry same-sex couples, in 2004, was which?
questions.note: Eleven years before the Supreme Court made it national. Vermont had civil unions first.

questions.q: Which state was the last to remove its ban on interracial marriage from its constitution, by a vote in 2000?
questions.note: Unenforceable since 1967. Forty percent still voted to keep it.

questions.q: Which ape species is known for defusing tension with sex, including between females?
questions.note: Food arrives, everyone gets tense, everyone has sex, everyone eats. Run by the females, too.

questions.q: Match.com, one of the first online dating sites, launched in what year?
questions.note: Dial-up speeds. You'd wait minutes for a photo you'd regret seeing.

questions.q: The word 'pornography' comes from Greek roots meaning what?
questions.note: Porne plus graphein. Coined in the 1800s when they dug up Pompeii and needed a shelf label.

questions.q: Lambskin condoms prevent pregnancy but do not reliably prevent what?
questions.note: Natural pores are big enough for viruses, too small for sperm. Read the box.

questions.q: The G-spot is named after which German gynecologist?
questions.note: He also invented an early IUD. He described the spot in 1950. The debate continues.

questions.q: The Kinsey scale rates sexual orientation on a scale of 0 to what?
questions.note: Zero is exclusively heterosexual, six exclusively homosexual. There's also an X for 'none.'

questions.q: Priapism, the condition in every Viagra warning, is named after a Greek god of what?
questions.note: Priapus, always depicted with a permanent and enormous erection. Patron saint of the 4-hour rule.

questions.q: Which rodent is science's go-to model for monogamy because it mates for life?
questions.note: Its cousin the meadow vole sleeps around. The difference is receptor density. Love is a brain region.

questions.q: In 2014, OkCupid admitted it had secretly experimented on users by doing what?
options: Telling bad matches they were great matches
questions.note: The blog post was titled 'We Experiment On Human Beings!' People kept swiping.

questions.q: In 2020, Utah reduced polygamy among consenting adults to what level of offense?
options: An infraction, like a traffic ticket
questions.note: Still a felony if fraud or abuse is involved. Otherwise, it's a fine.

questions.q: Adultery is still technically a felony in which state?
questions.note: Up to 3.5 years and $10,000. Nobody's been charged in decades. Still there.

questions.q: The word 'sadism' comes from the name of which French aristocrat?
questions.note: He spent 32 years in prisons and asylums and wrote the books there. Napoleon had him locked up.

questions.q: 'Masochism' is named after Leopold von Sacher-Masoch, a 19th-century Austrian who was a what?
questions.note: He wrote 'Venus in Furs.' He hated that the word was named after him. Which is fitting.

questions.q: A 2017 meta-analysis found sperm counts in Western men fell by roughly how much between 1973 and 2011?
questions.note: No sign of leveling off. The authors blamed chemicals, obesity and stress. So, everything.

questions.q: 'Blue balls' has an actual medical name. What is it?
questions.note: Yes, it's real. No, it's not dangerous. No, that's not an argument.

questions.q: The first country to legalize same-sex marriage, in 2001, was which?
questions.note: Four couples married at midnight in Amsterdam. The mayor officiated.

questions.q: Pompeii's best-preserved brothel is called the Lupanar, from the Latin for what?
questions.note: Lupa was slang for prostitute. Stone beds, erotic frescoes as a menu, and graffiti reviews.

questions.q: Speed dating was invented in 1998 by a what?
questions.note: Yaacov Deyo, to help Jewish singles in LA. Seven minutes, then a bell.

questions.q: Nike's 'Just Do It' slogan was inspired by the last words of whom?
options: A murderer facing a firing squad
questions.note: Gary Gilmore, Utah, 1977: 'Let's do it.' The ad man changed one word.

questions.q: Before acting, Steve Buscemi worked for four years as a what in New York?
questions.note: He went back to his old firehouse after 9/11 and dug for days. Didn't tell the press.

questions.q: Danny DeVito's Frank Reynolds joined It's Always Sunny in which season?
questions.note: FX said add a star or get cancelled. He came out of the couch and never left.

questions.q: Shane Gillis was fired from SNL in 2019 before his first episode. He first hosted the show in what year?
questions.note: His monologue told viewers not to Google why. Everyone Googled why.

questions.q: Fred Rogers kept his weight at exactly 143 pounds for decades. Why that number?
options: It spells 'I love you' in letter counts
questions.note: One letter, four letters, three letters. He swam daily to hold it. This man was not from here.

questions.q: Before 'The Joy of Painting,' Bob Ross spent 20 years as what?
questions.note: He was the guy screaming at recruits. He vowed never to raise his voice again.

questions.q: As a teenager, Christopher Walken worked in a circus as a what?
questions.note: The lioness was named Sheba. He says she was more like a dog. He was 16.

questions.q: The famous 'Wilhelm scream' stock sound effect is named after a character in what kind of movie?
questions.note: Private Wilhelm takes an arrow in the leg in 'The Charge at Feather River.' Reused in 400+ films.

questions.q: Brandon Lee, Bruce Lee's son, was killed on set in 1993 while filming which movie?
questions.note: A dummy bullet left in a prop gun. They finished the film with a double and early CGI.

questions.q: The LA medical examiner ruled Matthew Perry's 2023 death was caused by the acute effects of what?
questions.note: He was in legit ketamine therapy. The levels found were anesthesia-grade. Five people were charged.

questions.q: While filming Groundhog Day, Bill Murray was bitten twice by what?
questions.note: He needed rabies shots. 'Who the hell trained this gopher?'

questions.q: The mechanical shark in Jaws was nicknamed Bruce, after whom?
questions.note: It kept sinking in salt water. That's why you barely see it. That's why the movie works.

questions.q: The first video ever uploaded to YouTube, in 2005, is 18 seconds of a co-founder talking about what?
questions.note: 'The cool thing about these guys is they have really, really long trunks.' Civilization followed.

questions.q: In 2007, Keith Richards told NME he had snorted what, mixed with cocaine?
questions.note: He said it was a joke. Then his memoir said it was true. It's Keith Richards.

questions.q: Motley Crue's Nikki Sixx was declared dead for two minutes in 1987 after a heroin overdose. What song came out of it?
questions.note: Two adrenaline shots to the chest. He went home and shot up again that night.

questions.q: In 1965, Johnny Cash was sued by the federal government for accidentally doing what?
questions.note: His truck caught fire in Los Padres National Forest. He said he didn't care about 'your yellow buzzards.'

questions.q: In 1995, rapper Ol' Dirty Bastard took MTV cameras along to do what?
options: Pick up his welfare check in a limo
questions.note: He had a platinum record at the time. Food stamps and a check, then back in the limo.

questions.q: Richard Hatch, the first Survivor winner, went to prison for what?
options: Not paying taxes on his $1 million prize
questions.note: He claimed CBS had agreed to pay the tax. CBS had not. 51 months.

questions.q: Toy Story 2 was nearly lost in 1998 when someone ran a delete command on Pixar's servers. What saved it?
options: A backup on an employee's home computer
questions.note: The backups had been failing silently for a month. Galyn Susman was home with a newborn.

questions.q: Danny Trejo got into acting in 1985 because he was on a film set working as what?
options: A drug counselor for a cast member
questions.note: He'd done time in San Quentin. The screenwriter recognized him from prison. 400 movies later.

questions.q: In 2015, Nicolas Cage agreed to return a $276,000 purchase to Mongolia. What was it?
questions.note: He outbid Leonardo DiCaprio for it. It had been smuggled out. He was not charged.

questions.q: Shane Gillis's Netflix sitcom 'Tires' is set in what kind of business?
questions.note: Shot in Pennsylvania. Renewed for season two before season one even aired.

questions.q: The 'Nigerian prince' email scam is also called the 419 scam. What's the 419?
options: The fraud section of Nigeria's criminal code
The number of emails in the first batch
The area code it came from
questions.note: Advance-fee fraud. It predates email. It used to come by fax, and before that, by letter.

questions.q: In 2000, 50 Cent survived being shot how many times?
questions.note: Including once in the face. The fragment in his tongue gave him the slur.

questions.q: In 1848, railroad foreman Phineas Gage survived what passing completely through his skull?
questions.note: He sat up and talked. He lived 12 more years. Friends said he was 'no longer Gage.'

questions.q: Fecal transplants are an approved treatment for recurring infections of which bacterium?
questions.note: About 90 percent cure rate. The first FDA-approved version is an enema. Of someone else.

questions.q: The Tuskegee syphilis study, in which Black men were left untreated for research, ran until what year?
questions.note: Forty years. Penicillin was standard treatment by 1947. A whistleblower went to the press.

questions.q: HeLa cells, the first immortal human cell line, were taken in 1951 from a woman's what?
questions.note: Henrietta Lacks. No consent. They've been to space and helped make the polio vaccine.

questions.q: The chainsaw was originally invented in the 1780s to help with what?
questions.note: Cutting through the pelvis to get the baby out. Pre-anesthesia. Called symphysiotomy.

questions.q: In 2004 the FDA cleared which two living animals for sale as medical devices?
questions.note: Leeches for reattachment surgery, maggots for dead tissue. Both still in use.

questions.q: Which is the only US state with no seat belt law for adults?
questions.note: Live Free or Die. Mostly the second part.

questions.q: In the 1830s, an Ohio doctor sold what as a patent medicine in pill form?
questions.note: Dr. John Cook Bennett's tomato pills. Cured diarrhea, jaundice and indigestion, he said.

questions.q: In 2012, a Florida man died after winning a cockroach-eating contest. The prize was what?
questions.note: He choked on arthropod body parts. The python went to his estate.

questions.q: In 2009, which country issued a 100-trillion-dollar banknote?
questions.note: Worth about 30 US dollars at the time. Worth more than that now on eBay.

questions.q: Which is the only US state with a flag that isn't a rectangle?
questions.note: A swallowtail pennant. There's an official 17-step method for folding it.

questions.q: If you were at Point Nemo, the most remote spot in the ocean, the nearest humans would often be where?
questions.note: The ISS passes 250 miles overhead. Land is 1,670 miles away. Dead spacecraft get dumped there.

questions.q: From which US city can you drive directly south into Canada?
questions.note: Windsor, Ontario sits south of Detroit. The tunnel takes a few minutes.

questions.q: Which of these cities is farthest west?
questions.note: Reno beats LA by about 90 miles of longitude. Check a map, then check it again.

questions.q: Which US state is closest to Africa?
questions.note: Quoddy Head to Morocco, about 3,150 miles. The globe is round, which ruins everything.

questions.q: Which country has banned the sale of chewing gum since 1992?
questions.note: People stuck it on subway door sensors. Pharmacies can sell nicotine gum, with ID.

questions.q: Charles Osborne of Iowa holds the record for the longest attack of hiccups. How long?
questions.note: 1922 to 1990, roughly 430 million hiccups. He married twice and had eight kids.

questions.q: The record for the longest documented time without sleep, 11 days, was set in 1964 by a what?
questions.note: Randy Gardner, 17, for a science fair. Guinness stopped tracking it because people kept trying.

questions.q: Which US state eats the most Spam per person?
questions.note: About 7 million cans a year. It's on the McDonald's menu there.

questions.q: Ranch dressing was invented in the 1950s at an actual ranch in which state?
questions.note: Hidden Valley Ranch, near Santa Barbara. A plumber from Alaska mixed it for guests.

questions.q: Fortune cookies are nearly impossible to find in which country?
questions.note: They're Japanese, popularized by Japanese immigrants in California. China finds them weird.

questions.q: In 2024, it cost the US Mint roughly how much to make one penny?
questions.note: Nickels cost almost 14 cents. The Treasury finally ordered the last penny blanks in 2025.

questions.q: In 2011, which entire country could be rented for about $70,000 a night?
questions.note: Through Airbnb. Came with custom currency and temporary street signs with your name.

questions.q: Which country has more pyramids than Egypt?
questions.note: Around 200 at Meroe and elsewhere. Smaller, steeper. An Italian treasure hunter blew the tops off.

questions.q: Which US state is both the westernmost and the easternmost?
questions.note: The Aleutians cross the 180th meridian. Maine is furious.

questions.q: The island nation of Nauru briefly had the world's highest income per person in the 1970s thanks to mining what?
questions.note: Phosphate from millennia of guano. They strip-mined 80 percent of the island and the money's gone.

questions.q: Casu marzu, a Sardinian cheese, is famous for containing what?
questions.note: The larvae jump up to six inches. Illegal to sell in the EU, so a local will know a guy.

questions.q: Fredric Baur, who designed the Pringles can, was buried how in 2008?
options: At sea in a chip bag
questions.note: His kids stopped at Walgreens on the way to the funeral home to buy the can. Original flavor.

questions.q: The town of Dildo is in which Canadian province?
questions.note: Residents voted to keep the name in the 80s. Jimmy Kimmel is honorary mayor.

questions.q: The longest place name in the US, a 45-letter lake name, is in which state?
questions.note: Webster Lake. The road signs were misspelled for years. Nobody noticed because how would you.

questions.q: Which is the only US state capital without a McDonald's?
questions.note: Population about 8,000. There's a Burger King in the next town. Nobody's proud of that either.

questions.q: The Norwegian Arctic town of Longyearbyen has not allowed burials since 1950. Why?
questions.note: Bodies buried in 1918 still held traces of the flu virus. The dying get flown to the mainland.

questions.q: Who is banned from gambling at the Casino de Monte-Carlo?
questions.note: Since the 1800s. The princes wanted foreign money, not local ruin. Staff check your passport.
